title: Fine-Grained Pessimistic Locking over Distributed Aggregates
pattern: Acquiring separate pessimistic locks on multiple individual child components of a single domain aggregate across separate database shards or remote nodes, instead of acquiring a single lock on the aggregate root.
why_bad: Distributed locking is extremely expensive, introducing network round-trip overhead and disk forces (fsync) for each lock [185, 301]. Locking child entities individually increases network traffic, amplifies transaction latency, and dramatically raises the probability of concurrent lock contention and distributed deadlock [87, 88]. It also exposes the child entities to inconsistent partial updates if any lock acquisition fails mid-way [87, 296].
detection: Identify consecutive remote lock acquisitions or updates directed to different logical tables that are causally nested within a single Domain-Driven Design aggregate (e.g., Cargo, Delivery History, Handling Events), where the updates are not encapsulated under a single transaction root.
fix: Structure data around clean Aggregate boundaries. Enforce a single Coarse-Grained Lock on the Aggregate Root or represent child updates as a single, atomic document update on a single shard [74, 88].
source: Eric Evans, *Domain-Driven Design*, Chapter 7 (Aggregates) / passages [87, 88]; Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 9 / passage [185]; Martin Fowler, *Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture*, Chapters 7 & 16 / passage [296, 301].
